newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway banks profit from non-core business.
newsitem.headline: Norway banks profit from non-core business.

text.p: Norway's three largest banks on Tuesday booked first-quarter profits that beat market forecasts thanks mainly to higher-than-expected income from non-core business, analysts said.
The banks also saw income from foreign exchange trading boosted by a fluctuating Norwegian crown in the first three months.

Den norske Bank (DnB), the country's top bank, said its net result rose 54 million crowns to 820 million crowns from the same 1996 period. It was mainly strengthened by a 27 percent rise to 856 million in profits from operations other than interest on loans, its traditional source of income.

Christiania Bank og Kreditkasse, Norway's number two bank, said operating profit before loan losses rose 19 percent from the corresponding 1996 period to 592 million crowns. It was the second best such figure in the bank's history thanks partly to it's non-interest income soaring 35 percent to 511 million.

Union Bank of Norway (UBN), the third largest bank and the biggest savings bank, recorded an operating profit after losses of 360 million crowns, a drop of about 10 percent. But the result was better than market forecasts and non-interest operating income was up 16 percent at 481 million crowns.
The shares of all three banks rose in afternoon trade on the Oslo Stock Exchange.
The banks, competing in a crowded financial market, have struggled for three years against shrinking interest margins.

The tightening margins have squeezed net interest income despite higher loan volumes and forcing the banks to focus more on other means of income, such as foreign exchange trading, real estate and insurance operations, according to analysts.
"They have diversified the income structure and have more legs to stand on," an Oslo-based analyst said. "The bank scenario looks very good. The Christiania result was extremely strong."
DnB's booked a net interest income of 1.06 billion crowns in the first quarter, largely stable from last year, as higher volumes offset the effect of the squeeze on margins.
For Christiania, net interest income rose three percent to 884 million crowns.

"The bank's income side shows a positive development, and particularly the activities in Christiania Markets and the bank's funds management area contribute to the increased income," a Christiania statement said.
Kjell Kran, UBN Chief Executive Officer, was pleased.

"While interest income has been reduced as a result of the competition in the market, income from subsidiaries has become an increasingly important part of the bank's earnings," Kran said. "We believe this development makes the bank more robust and better able to tackle short-term market fluctuations."

DnB said it saw healthy gains in profits from trading in foreign exchange and financial instruments and brisk stock market activity resulted in high commission income from securities trading and custodial services.
"The fluctuating crown opens for income for the banks both from customer trading and own-account trading," an analyst said.
Christiania said net gains from foreign exchange and financial derivatives were doubled at 124 million crowns.

"The reason for these comparatively high gains on foreign exchange and derivatives is in particular the good performance in the bank's own trading in the foreign exchange and interest rate markets," Christiania said in a statement.
Christiania plans to merge with Norway's biggest insurance company Storebrand ASA this year to take over DnB's role as the biggest financial institution in the country.
Unlike the banks, Storebrand disappointed the markets with first-quarter book profits of 141 million crowns, down by more than 40 percent because of lower financial income in non-life insurance.
